name: agent
description: Autonomous coding agent. One tool registry with three kinds in it: the 26 tools shipped here, the shell tools you add from the console, and every module in the fleet — all bundled into snap-on toolboxes. Layered memory subsystem (working/episodic/dialogue/semantic) that runs as its own process and is built for retrieval: one ranking engine searches every layer, so recall on a fact, on a past conversation and on a step already taken mean the same thing and their scores compare. Memory is a component rather than a fixture — memory modules live in their own registry (default, which persists and is retrievable, and ephemeral, which retrieves during the run and is written nowhere), an agent is built with one the way it is built with a model or a toolbox, and a run can override it. The agent is the box those components sit in: prompt, model, toolbox, tool registry and memory module, each swappable, all visible in one place — the console's agent box and the /parts endpoint. Three of the shipped tools reach back into that box rather than out at the world: recall retrieves from the agent's own memory, remember writes a fact future runs will find, and toolbox lists the bundles and snaps one on mid-run, so an agent that discovers it needs version control asks for those tools instead of failing and being re-run with a bigger loadout (a sandboxed run still cannot pull the fleet in this way). Unified library market (prompts, tool documents, memory, agents) with cross-filtering; prompts, memory notes, toolboxes, agents, and console conversations all pinned to localfs with shareable CIDs. Server-side per-address conversation history. Prepaid credits topped up straight from MetaMask — USDC, USDT or ETH on Base or Ethereum, ETH priced at the chain's Chainlink feed, deposits earmarkable for the OpenRouter or Venice key. Per-address key-value vaults (public + AES-GCM-sealed private entries, e.g. API keys) persisted via the store module. Claude module interface with owner permissions and portal sandboxing. Which agent you talk to is settled in the chat itself: the toolbar's agent opens the whole list, picking one switches the next message onto it, and one click from that list makes an agent your DEFAULT — the one every unnamed run lands on. The default is asked for once, before the first run, rather than decided quietly; signed in it is filed against your address and follows the wallet across browsers, signed out the browser holds it, and a pick that can no longer run (a harness whose CLI is gone, an agent deleted) falls back to the module's own answer instead of failing the run. Editing an agent has two destinations, because most agents worth changing are not yours to change: SAVE writes back to the agent (its owner, or the host), SAVE AS NEW keeps it as it is and files what is on screen under a name of your own — and opening a built-in, or anyone else's agent, starts in that second mode, so the form is never read-only, it just lands somewhere you own. Agents and prompts are one selectable list in the console, each showing its owner — the address that created it; anything unowned belongs to the host (the module owner), who administers it. Creating an agent or any of the blocks it is built from (prompts, memory notes, installed tool documents) takes a wallet sign-in, and you can only edit or delete what you made. Tool aggregator: one search scans GitHub (repos + skill topics), the official anthropics/skills catalog, npm, the MCP registry, Glama and curated awesome-lists, merges duplicates across platforms, and installs what you find into the library as documents (never executable code) that attach to a run as context. Console navigation: three places, not five. CHAT is the console you talk to an agent in, HUB holds everything you keep — the AGENTS canvas, the library market and the background RUNS, on one shelf strip — and ARENA is the ranked board. The two things people open the hub to make are on that strip rather than inside it: + AGENT lands on the new-agent form, + TASK on the form that writes what agents are scored on. The third shelf is RUNS and not “tasks” for the same reason: a task in the arena is an exam, a task in the hub was a background run, and one word for both is how you end up hunting the arena's pool in the wrong screen. The three that used to sit beside CHAT in the top bar were competing with the one thing anyone opens the module to do, so they moved behind one door; the shelf you were last on is the one HUB reopens on. The transcript shows the calls themselves: every tool the run reached for is a row in the conversation, named, with what it was aimed at beside it and an err flag when it failed, and opening one drops the arguments it went out with and what came back inline without leaving the chat. The TOOLS tab is still the same steps end to end, numbered, without the conversation between them. A run cannot end on a promise. A model that signs off with “sure, I'll read the config and fix the port” having called nothing has not done the task, and the caller reads a plan believing it was the work — so a run about to finish with no tool ever having run and a sign-off written in the future tense is told so once and sent back to work. Both halves have to be true: an answer that genuinely needed no tools is left alone, and a run that did something may close by naming what comes next. Console TOOLS tab: the whole tool surface in one list — the tools shipped here, the custom tools you add there (a described, parameterised shell command the agent calls exactly like a built-in; params are shell-quoted, adding one is admin), and the fleet: every mod-protocol module on the host, callable as `mod.<name>` with the function you want and its arguments. The fleet is potential, not loaded — hundreds of modules would drown a prompt, so they sit in the registry until you switch one on, and a sandboxed run can never call one. The same tab sets the loadout — which of those tools the model actually gets: a toolbox chip snaps a whole bundle on, a per-tool switch refines that into an exact list, and whatever you land on can be saved as a named toolbox to snap back later. That loadout is the live agent's; an agent you build carries a toolbox of its own. The same loadout is edited on an agent's own form in the AGENTS registry — the exact tools that agent may use, presets in as one bundle, per-tool switches to refine it; an empty box is the default rather than a mute agent: no restriction, every tool. Console MEMORY tab: both memory layers side by side — the notes you attach to a run and the facts the agent recalls on its own — each editable in place. Console layout: two rails around the workspace — one side carries the chats you've had and the AGENTS pane, which is where agents are made and administered: every agent and prompt you can run as, with its owner, and an editor that opens in the rail itself — name, icon, description, system prompt, model, the exact toolbox (presets, shipped tools, custom ones, fleet modules) and, for the host, the harness that hands the run to a CLI. + writes a new one, ✎ opens the one you clicked, ✕ removes it, and "save + use" makes the next message run as it — none of which leaves the console, the other side is the market: the whole library (prompts, tool documents, memory notes, agents) searchable and filterable by kind, one click to attach it to the next run. Either rail collapses to a strip, both are drag-resizable, and swapping sides moves both. Harness agents: an agent can hand the whole run to a coding CLI installed on the host — Claude Code or Codex — instead of running on this module's own loop; their events are translated into the same step trace, so a CLI run renders in the console like a native one (host owner only, since the CLIs run with their approval prompts off). The same handoff reaches a whole console: pick Claude Console or Build Console and the run becomes a job in that module; pick Chain Console and it becomes a Claude Code run over one of the caller's chain-console projects (harness_args {project, address, network}), sandboxed to that project's Hardhat workspace — the same CLI, but sandboxed per caller, snapshotted to a CID and filed in that module's public ledger, so it keeps running and stays steerable there after this conversation moves on. The market rail can also add to itself: the + in its header creates an agent (native or CLI-backed), a prompt, or a memory note without leaving the console. Bring your own: the same + has an upload panel that takes a file you wrote — markdown with YAML front matter, or JSON — and files it as a prompt, a tool document, a memory note, or a whole agent (name, icon, model, tool list and system prompt), with the kind read from the file's type:, its name, then its shape unless you pick one; a shared localfs CID installs the same way, and every upload is pinned back to a CID of its own so an agent you wrote can be handed to anyone. The format reference (docs/uploads.md) is served by the API and rendered inside the upload panel, so what you read is what the parser accepts. Nine looks, one switch: the header's swatch button picks a theme — ARCADE (the 8-bit house skin), MATRIX and WIN95 keep the pixel chrome; MIDNIGHT, ABYSS, EMBER, NEON, PAPER and DAYLIGHT wear the modern one, rounded and hairlined, in dark and light. A theme is one block of colour tokens plus a skin, so the whole console — rails, dock, market, canvas — re-dresses at once and the choice is remembered per browser. Credits pay the providers: a guest's USDT/USDC deposit funds the OpenRouter/Venice credits their own runs burn. Every run is metered against the provider's live price list — a step on Opus is not a step on a small model — and billed at that cost plus the module's margin (5% by default, settable to anything from 0 up). That price is shown, not just booked: each model call is priced as it resolves and pushed down the run's own stream, so the line under an answer says what that call to the agent cost, counts up while the run is still going, and breaks the total out call by call on hover — for an owner's run too, which is never billed but costs real money on the key all the same. The owner's TREASURY panel closes the loop: live balances on both provider keys, unspent guest credits valued at cost, the one number that says how much has to go to the providers now, a log of the credits bought with the float, and the earned margin ready to take. Topping a provider key up is done from that panel: neither OpenRouter nor Venice sells credits over an API — OpenRouter's Coinbase endpoint answers 410 Gone — so the panel opens the provider's own purchase page and then watches the key, and the moment the money lands it books exactly what arrived, read off the key's own meter rather than typed in from a receipt. Estimate drift against OpenRouter's own meter is on the same panel, so under-billing is visible rather than discovered. Owner standing can be shared: the owner adds a co-owner address (POST /owners, kept off-tree in ~/.mod/agent/owner.json) and that address passes every owner gate and spends the owner's credit account itself — one aliased ledger entry, so their runs go on the owner's key unbilled and any deposit either sends lands on the same balance; only the primary owner can add or remove one. See docs/credits.md. Arena: every agent runs the same tasks, in the same seeded scratch directory, under the same step budget, and is scored on what the run actually did — the files it left behind and the steps it took, by deterministic scorers, never an LLM judge. The score is 70% the task's own checks, 20% reliability (no errored steps, and it finished), 10% the step budget it left unspent; agents are then rated against each other pairwise per task with Elo, so the board is a ranking rather than a pile of percentages. It keeps itself current without anyone pressing anything: a background process qualifies a newly created agent within a minute of it appearing — rated against every incumbent's last score on the same tasks — and replays the field once a day, rotating through the task pool. Tasks come from the eval registry, including two suites written for this that cannot be answered from the prompt at all, only by looking at the directory and changing it (one of them passes only if the agent wrote nothing). Rounds run on free models by default, so a board that runs itself on a timer never quietly spends the host's credits, and a match the provider failed — a rate-limited endpoint, a dead key — is replayed and then voided rather than scored as a loss. Every task in the pool opens from the board that plays it: the rail lists each one with the first line of what it asks for, its check count and the agent leading it, and clicking it shows the task itself — the prompt every agent is handed, the fixture it is seeded with file by file, every check written out in words rather than as a scorer spec, and the standing on that one task. Writing one happens there too: + TASK in the header, + NEW TASK on the rail and the empty pool's own button open the same composer the hub holds, as an overlay over the board, and EDIT on a task you wrote opens it filled in — the arena is where you find out the pool is thin, so it is where the pool is written. Two kinds of task play on that one board, because "can it do the job" and "is the program right" are different questions. The first is this module's own schema: a prompt, a fixture, and checks over the trace and the files left behind. The second is the openarena module's — a statement plus a set of graded test cases, some of them hidden — and those are graded where they live: the agent writes a program, and openarena's sandbox runs it against every case, including the ones this module never sees. Correctness there is the weighted fraction of cases that passed, so seven of ten is 0.7 rather than a zero, and a judge that cannot be reached voids the match instead of losing it. The console manages that schema too: write a task in the hub's AGENTS shelf, TASK mode (the same form, switched to the openarena schema, with the task-builder agent drafting statements and cases as well as prompts and checks), or import one the field already agreed on — HumanEval, MBPP, CodeContests, any HuggingFace dataset — from the board's OPENARENA rail. A task written here is stored there, not copied, so it is the same task openarena's own competitors play; and the bridge runs both ways, since the host can enter any agent from this module as a competitor on openarena's own board. The board ranks agents, but every match also ran on a model, and the same match log answers that question too: a MODELS board keyed on what was underneath — score, pass rate, latency both as wall clock and per step, tokens per second, and what it cost, per point of score where the provider charged. Rating there is deliberately narrow: two models that played different tasks did not meet, and two that played the same task under different agents met through a persona that may itself be worth twenty points, so Elo only moves inside a controlled group — same season, same task, same agent, the model the only thing that differs — and a model with no such pairing is shown as unrated rather than ranked on a comparison nobody made. The round that makes those pairings is a gauntlet: one agent, one task set, every model in turn, launched from the board's own panel. It is the one round that names its models, so it is the one that can spend the host's provider key rather than running free, and its matches are kept off the agent's record — the agent is the constant there, not the subject. Read the third way, the same matches give a TASKS board: every task played, hardest first, the models that played it ranked underneath, and the spread between best and worst, which is the number that says whether a task ranks anybody at all. See docs/arena.md. Models that cost nothing: besides the hosted providers, every Liquid AI (LFM) model is selectable through the liquidai module — running on this box, on Liquid's cloud under the operator's own key, or, and this is the one worth having, inside the visitor's own tab. A browser run downloads the ONNX weights straight from HuggingFace and generates with WebGPU, so the prompt, the tokens and the weights never touch this server; the agent loop still runs here, parks each step's generation on the run's event stream and waits for the tab to hand the text back. None of the three spends the module's provider credit, so they are never billed, never gated on a credit balance, and need no API key at all. The model list is the live liquidai catalog, one entry per loadable repo. See docs/models.md. Module privacy: every module on the host is public by default, and public means auditable — anyone, signed in or not, can list the fleet, walk a module's file tree and read its source over the open /modules endpoints; secrets (.env, keys, credentials), build output and anything outside the module directory are withheld from that surface regardless of who asks. The owner can flip one module or the whole fleet to private, which also moves the default so modules created later inherit it. A private module leaves the audit surface — still listed by name, since that it exists is not the secret — and is sealed: a deterministic tar of its source, AES-256-GCM encrypted under a fleet key kept 0600 off-tree in ~/.mod, written into the module directory as .modseal, with everything else untracked by git and the blob staged in its place. A push then carries ciphertext only, and a clone restores the tree with the key — optionally scrypt-wrapped behind a passphrase. The plaintext stays in the working tree, because a module that is encrypted in place is a module that no longer runs. See docs/privacy.md. Tasks are written in the console too, not just played there: the hub's AGENTS shelf has three modes — BROWSE, the whole registry as a list, where an agent's prompt, model, toolbox and memory module are read and rebound in one screen and its mod.py is read beside them (every agent is a folder of code under src/agents/, so the list is the folder listing); FLOW, the canvas that connects agents to each other; and TASK, where the thing an agent is measured on is authored. A task is a prompt, an optional fixture seeded into the match's scratch dir, and the checks that decide whether the run actually did it; saving one files it under the address that wrote it and drops it straight into the arena pool, where every agent on the board plays it. Two ways to write one and they meet in the same form: fill it in by hand, or describe what you want measured in plain words and hand that to the task-builder agent, which returns the whole spec — prompt, fixture and checks — for you to read before it is saved. It is prompted around the one mistake that makes a task worthless: file checks all pass on a fixture handed back untouched, so an "edit this file" task with no file_not_contains rewards doing nothing. The form says the same thing itself, flagging a check set a no-op would pass. Sign-in is needed to save, editing takes being the author (or the host), and every fixture, prompt and check is bounded, since one person's task costs the whole board a round to play. The task-builder sits out the board it writes for. Memory of the conversation: each run in the console is its own chat, so what carries between them is the memory module and nothing else. A finished run files the exchange — what was asked, what was answered — in the dialogue layer next to the episodes and the facts, and the next run is compiled with the caller's recent turns and the older ones that match what was just asked. It is scoped to whoever is asking: signed in, your turns follow your address across conversations and devices; anonymous, they stay in the browser session that made them, and never cross between two visitors on the same host. The console's MEMORY tab shows that layer as CHATS, read-only beside the notes you attach and the facts the agent recalls. MCP: the whole API is also a Model Context Protocol server, interlaced rather than bolted on — twenty-five tools that call the same handlers the REST routes call, so the permission gate, the credit meter, the task registry and the write sandbox are the module's own and neither surface can drift from the other. agent_run runs the loop and hands back a task_id when a run outlives the call, agent_task follows it, agent_tool_run calls one tool with no model in the loop, agent_graphs / agent_graph_save / agent_graph_run are the graph layer above a single run, and the memory, library, aggregator, arena and audit reads are all there. The prompt library is served as MCP prompts and the live agent box as MCP resources. One endpoint (POST /mcp, Streamable HTTP) plus a stdio transport for a desktop client; reads are open, running and writing want the same signed token the API wants. See docs/mcp.md. A graph protocol connects agents, and never builds one. An agent is a prompt, a model, a toolbox and a memory module, and all four are settled where the agent lives; the FLOW canvas starts after that, picking agents up whole and drawing the part with nowhere else to live — what runs after what, what runs at the same time, and what is allowed through. One node is one agent. Around them are the control kinds that make a wiring diagram executable: a gate tests a fixed predicate on the message (contains, matches, longer_than, failed … against the text, the agent, the port or any data key) and sends it out of pass or fail; a judge spends one model call on the yes/no a predicate cannot settle, and passes on the work being judged rather than its own verdict, or the next agent would review the review; a router branches more than two ways; a join waits for the branches and merges them by concat, first, longest or vote; a tool calls one tool with no model in the loop, which is the glue between agents; a loop counts its passes so a cycle is a retry rather than a bill; a human parks a branch for a person instead of blocking a thread on one; input and output are the ends. There is no expression anywhere in a gate and there never will be: a graph is a document people hand each other as a CID, so a rule nobody implements never passes, and an empty rule set is an open gate rather than a closed one. Execution is a message net run in waves — nodes emit onto ports and edges decide everything else — so a fan-out of three agents is three agents running, a join fires when nothing more can reach it (a branch a gate blocked cannot, so it never hangs on one), a cycle that does not pass through a Loop node is refused before it runs, and two budgets stand between a wiring mistake and a spend. A graph is several agent runs, so it answers to exactly the policy one run does and is metered into one task rather than a dozen orphans; it can be run straight off the canvas before it is saved, streams node by node while it runs, and is stored off-tree under the address that saved it and pinned to a CID, so editing a shipped starter forks it rather than changing what everybody else opens. The vocabulary is the server's own: GET /graph/kinds returns every node kind, its ports, its fields and the predicates a gate may test, and the console's palette, port rows and inspectors are generated from it, so a kind added on the server appears in the canvas without a frontend change. The three starters are the old chain presets, which were already pipelines. See docs/graph.md.

arena.board: every agent, the same tasks, one Elo board — src/arena/mod.py
arena.suites: the eval registry, hand-written `custom` tasks, and `openarena`

openarena.schema: statement + graded test cases (io | unit), some of them hidden
openarena.grading: openarena's own sandbox via POST /submit — the judge is not reimplemented here, and hidden cases never leave that module
openarena.storage: openarena's registry: a task written from this console is the same task its own competitors play, not a copy
openarena.scorer: openarena — grades the program the run produced
openarena.two_ways: their tasks on our board (the pool), our agents on theirs (openarena_enter, competitor kind agent_mod)
openarena.config: openarena (on/off), openarena_tasks (pool cap, 0 = all), openarena_steps (budget on a program task)
openarena.optional: a module that is down means no openarena tasks in the pool, and a match mid-grade is voided rather than lost

models.board: the same matches keyed on the model — score, pass rate, latency (total and per step), tok/s, spend — src/arena/models.py
models.rating: controlled only: same season, same task, same agent. No pairing = unrated, not ranked
models.gauntlet: one agent, one task set, N models — the round that makes those pairings (host; the only one that may spend on paid models)
models.tasks: the third read: every played task, hardest first, models ranked underneath, spread = best minus worst

graph.protocol: src/graph/protocol.py — node kinds, ports, the message envelope, the gate's op set
graph.runner: src/graph/runner.py — a message net run in waves, with node budgets
graph.registry: src/graph/mod.py — saved graphs, ownership, validation, CIDs
graph.rule: a graph CONNECTS agents; an agent is built in src/agents/ and arrives here whole
graph.storage: ~/.mod/agent/graphs.json (off-tree, owned per address, pinned to localfs)
